name: Privacy
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Pseudonymous Is Not the Same as Anonymous
lesson.summary: Public blockchains reveal every transaction to everyone, forever, and addresses only look anonymous; real privacy requires additional cryptographic techniques layered on top of the base ledger.
lesson.body:
Recall Trust: a blockchain earns trust partly through radical transparency, since every participant can independently verify the entire history for themselves. But transparency and privacy pull in opposite directions. A public blockchain like Bitcoin or Ethereum publishes every transaction, every amount, and every sending and receiving address to anyone in the world, permanently, with no built-in way to redact anything later, a tension this chapter batch returns to directly in Right to Be Forgotten.

A common misconception is that blockchain addresses provide anonymity, since they are strings of letters and numbers rather than names. In reality they provide pseudonymity: an address is not your name, but it is a stable, traceable identifier. Once a single transaction links an address to a real identity, an exchange's identity-verification record, an IP address logged when a transaction was broadcast, a payment to a known merchant, or simply reusing the same address repeatedly, analysts can often work backward and deanonymize the entire transaction history tied to that address. Blockchain analysis firms and law enforcement agencies do exactly this as routine practice, clustering addresses by spending patterns to map them to real-world entities.

Recall Encryption: encryption protects data from parties who do not hold the decryption key, but a public blockchain's entire design point is that every node can read the ledger in order to verify it, so simply encrypting transaction contents would break the model, since nodes could no longer check that an encrypted transaction was actually valid. This is precisely the gap dedicated privacy technologies exist to fill: letting the network verify that a transaction is correct without seeing its details.

A concrete example makes the stakes clear. An employee paid in cryptocurrency at a publicly visible address has effectively published their salary, and every later payment they make from that address, to anyone willing to look it up on a public block explorer. Compare this to a bank account, where the ledger is private by default and disclosed only through specific legal processes. This gap between what a public ledger exposes and what people actually want kept private is the direct motivation for serious privacy technology, ring signatures, confidential transaction amounts, and especially the zero-knowledge proofs covered in the next chapter.
